clips.text_en_b1: If you had to hold only one asset for the next 10 years, would you choose Bitcoin or gold? The poster asked /biz/ which is better. Some said BTC will eat gold's store-of-value role. Others said gold has 5,000 years of trust. What actually wins long-term, and why?
clips.source_hint: biz thread asking BTC vs gold for 10-year hold

signal.rationale: OP frames BTC vs gold as a long-horizon store-of-value bet, implicitly bullish on BTC

clips.text_en_b2: If you were forced to hold just one asset for the next decade, would you go with Bitcoin or gold? The poster put this question to /biz/, and the responses split sharply. Some anons argued BTC will gradually eat into gold's traditional store-of-value role, while others countered that gold carries five thousand years of proven trust. The deeper question is what actually holds up long-term, and on what grounds.
clips.text_en_c1: Were you compelled to retain a single asset for the coming decade, would your preference fall upon Bitcoin or gold? A recent /biz/ inquiry posed precisely this dilemma, igniting a fervent exchange among respondents. One faction contended that BTC would inevitably cannibalise gold's longstanding store-of-value function, whereas another invoked gold's five-millennium track record of institutional trust. Beneath the rhetoric lies a more pressing consideration: if one were already incurring losses on both instruments, the calculus might shift from absolute conviction to relative harm minimisation. The thread remains unresolved, which is, perhaps, the most honest verdict of all.
clips.text_en_c2: Were one compelled to allocate capital to a single asset for the coming decade, the perennial Bitcoin-versus-gold debate reasserts itself with particular urgency on /biz/. Proponents of BTC contend that its programmable scarcity and network effects will inexorably cannibalise gold's millennia-old function as a monetary reserve, whereas gold advocates invoke five thousand years of accumulated trust, a track record no protocol can replicate. The original poster, nursing losses on both positions, frames the dilemma less as a question of conviction than as a comparative exercise in determining which holding will depreciate more gracefully. Whether the triumph belongs to the digital insurgent or the ancient store of value remains, ultimately, a question that every allocator must answer for themselves.

clips.text_zh: 又中🙏 BTC橫盤幾星期唔理，pump 15%之後個個湧入。即係我哋啲early都係執死雞？wtf lol
clips.text_en_b1: Why does everyone want to buy BTC after the move already happened? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. The poster says this pattern repeats every cycle and retail always arrives late.
clips.source_hint: biz thread about retail FOMO buying BTC after the pump

signal.rationale: Post-hoc observation about retail behaviour, no actionable setup

clips.text_en_b2: Why does retail always pile in once the move has already happened? You sit through weeks of BTC going nowhere and completely tune it out, then it suddenly pumps 15% and everyone scrambles to get in. The poster points out this pattern repeats every single cycle, and ordinary investors consistently show up far too late to catch the real upside.
clips.text_en_c1: It is a phenomenon so predictable it borders on ritual: Bitcoin consolidates sideways for weeks, attracting virtually no retail interest whatsoever, before staging a sudden 15% surge that triggers an immediate avalanche of FOMO-driven entries. The original poster on /biz/ articulates a frustration that resonates across every preceding cycle, namely that retail capital consistently arrives after the substantial move has already materialised. Those positioned early, it transpires, are perpetually scrambling to extract remaining gains whilst latecoments absorb the volatility. Whether this pattern reflects genuine behavioural finance principles or merely collective amnesia remains, charitably speaking, an open question.
clips.text_en_c2: It is a phenomenon as predictable as it is maddening: Bitcoin consolidates for weeks on end, attracting scarcely a sidelong glance from retail participants, and then, once price has appreciated by some fifteen percent in a brisk upward thrust, the very same cohort descends en masse, intoxicated by the prospect of catching a move already substantially underway. The poster, having positioned himself early, observes with weary bemusement that the early birds are effectively scavenging scraps, while latecomers, convinced they are participating in some bold contrarian entry, are in fact the most obedient of momentum-chasing sheep. This ritual recurs with metronomic regularity across every cycle, and one suspects retail will never quite manage to arrive before the move rather than after it.

It says that as AI replaces human labor, wealth concentrates heavily in the hands of a tiny group of capital owners. When inequality hits a critical mass, the ruling elite will use AI to repress workers instead of sharing the gains.

clips.text_en_b2: A Nobel-winning MIT economist has published a paper titled 'Automation and Repression,' and its implications are genuinely unsettling. The core argument is that as AI steadily displaces human labor, wealth concentrates heavily in the hands of a tiny group of capital owners. Once inequality crosses a critical threshold, the ruling elite will deploy AI to suppress workers rather than redistribute the gains, hollowing out democracy in the process.
clips.text_en_c1: A Nobel laureate from MIT has authored a paper entitled 'Automation and Repression', the implications of which are profoundly unsettling. The central thesis argues that as artificial intelligence progressively supplants human labour, the resultant economic surplus accrues disproportionately to a minuscule cadre of capital holders. Once inequality surpasses a critical threshold, the ruling class, rather than redistributing gains, will presumably deploy AI infrastructure to surveil, pacify, and ultimately subjugate displaced workers. For those still pursuing professional licensing, the timing is exquisite: one may complete a decade of qualification only to be rendered obsolete by an algorithm that, incidentally, never required a certification in the first place.
clips.text_en_c2: A Nobel-laureate economist from MIT has circulated a paper bearing the sober title 'Automation and Repression,' whose argument warrants far closer attention than its grim conclusion might initially invite. The thesis runs thus: as artificial intelligence progressively supplants human labour across an ever-wider swathe of productive activity, the resulting surplus accrues disproportionately to a vanishingly small stratum of capital holders, while displaced workers receive neither meaningful recompense nor political accommodation. Once inequality crosses a critical threshold, the paper contends, ruling elites will deploy precisely those same AI systems to surveil, constrain, and ultimately repress the dispossessed, rather than permitting any redistribution that might dilute their consolidated advantage. Whether democratic institutions possess the resilience to forestall such an outcome remains, for the moment, an open and deeply uncomfortable question.

clips.text_zh: BYD贏咗🧐 美國財長想踩中國補貼，點知全世界淨係記住「$70k嘅車$35k買到」。BYD今次免費宣傳抵過畀錢賣廣告 lol
clips.text_en_b1: US Treasury Secretary Bessent tried to slam China over BYD subsidies. He said 'BYD is the best $70,000 car that $35,000 can buy.' The /pol/ thread notes the only thing people actually heard was that BYD is a great car at half the price. Best free ad for BYD in 2026.
clips.source_hint: pol thread on Bessent accidentally advertising BYD
clips.text_en_b2: US Treasury Secretary Bessent tried to take a swipe at China over BYD subsidies, but the plan spectacularly backfired. He boasted that BYD is essentially the best $70,000 car money can buy, available for just $35,000. The /pol/ thread points out that audiences across the world walked away remembering one thing: BYD offers serious value at roughly half the price. It turned into the cheapest ad campaign of 2026.
clips.text_en_c1: In what may rank as 2026's most spectacular own-goal in geopolitical communication, US Treasury Secretary Bessent intended to excoriate Chinese industrial subsidies, only to inadvertently furnish BYD with a masterclass in inadvertent brand amplification. His assertion that BYD represents 'the finest seventy-thousand-dollar automobile that thirty-five thousand dollars can acquire' was ostensibly a critique; the global takeaway, however, proved rather less nuanced. Across /pol/, the consensus is unanimous: the remark functioned as free advertising of a calibre that no paid campaign could conceivably replicate, cementing BYD's value proposition in the collective consciousness without expending a single marketing dollar.
clips.text_en_c2: Treasury Secretary Bessent evidently intended his critique of Chinese industrial subsidisation to land as a withering indictment of BYD, the electric-vehicle manufacturer whose global ascendancy has occasioned no small measure of anxiety in Washington. Instead, his carefully chosen formulation, that BYD represents 'the best seventy-thousand-dollar car that thirty-five thousand dollars can buy,' has propagated across the internet as perhaps the most exquisitely unintentional endorsement in recent automotive memory. The /pol/ thread captures the irony with suitable relish: whatever the Secretary's policy objections, the only datum that has lodged itself in the collective consciousness is that a genuinely superior vehicle can be acquired at half its implicit Western price. BYD has, quite inadvertently, secured what amounts to the most valuable advertisement of 2026, gratis.

clips.text_en_b2: With S15 underway once again, a /v/ poster raises a familiar frustration: whenever developers publish clear, reasonable rules, Western teams seem incapable of simply following them. The argument is that these squads consistently hunt for edge cases and loopholes, while Eastern teams tend to play within the intended boundaries. The thread links to a recent League of Legends controversy where pro players pushed the rules to breaking point.
clips.text_en_c1: As the League of Legends S15 championship approaches, an inevitable spectacle reasserts itself: Western organisations apparently incapable of adhering to plainly articulated regulations. A /v/ thread catalogues the perennial frustration whereby game developers establish ostensibly reasonable parameters, only for Western rosters to embark upon forensic interpretations of edge cases and semantic loopholes. Eastern counterparts, by contrast, demonstrate the curious discipline of actually following instructions as written. Whether this reflects divergent cultural attitudes toward authority, a competitive calculus that rewards boundary-testing, or simply an inability to parse plain English remains hotly contested, though the pattern itself is empirically indisputable.
clips.text_en_c2: With the S15 League of Legends championship looming, a /v/ thread returns to a question that has acquired the quality of seasonal ritual: why is it that Western teams so reliably contrive to discover the precise outer boundary of any competently drafted rulebook? The original poster argues, with evident exasperation, that developers promulgate sensible guidelines, whereupon Eastern organisations absorb them as written and compete accordingly, whereas their Western counterparts, possessed of an apparently irrepressible interpretive impulse, set about mining every conceivable edge case until the rule in question requires a public clarification. The linked controversy concerns precisely such an instance, and the weary consensus holds that this pattern, far from being incidental, has become structural.

clips.text_en_b2: A /fit/ thread asks how often anyone actually witnesses a 405 lbs bench press in their gym, and the replies paint a fairly bleak picture. At commercial gyms it almost never happens, while even hardcore powerlifting gyms might see it once or twice a year at best. A few anons mention that when someone does rep it, the entire floor stops dead to watch the spectacle unfold.
clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ thread poses a deceptively simple inquiry: how frequently does one actually witness a 405-pound bench press in a commercial gymnasium? The responses, drawn from accumulated collective experience, suggest the figure hovers near zero in chain fitness establishments, perhaps manifesting once or thrice annually in dedicated powerlifting facilities where such lifts constitute the cultural baseline. Several anons recount singular encounters wherein a lone individual executed the lift, prompting the entire facility to suspend activity in collective reverence. For those whose overhead press remains, shall we say, aspirational, the timeline to respectable numbers appears distressingly geological in scope.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ thread poses what initially appears a frivolous question but proves rather more revealing upon reflection: how frequently does one actually witness a four-hundred-and-five-pound bench press in one's own gym? The consensus, assembled from anons across the commercial-fitness landscape, converges on the disappointing observation that such feats are vanishingly rare in ordinary establishments, perhaps occurring once or twice a year even in dedicated powerlifting facilities. A handful of respondents report that their gym harbours precisely one such individual, whose working sets invariably attract a deferential audience momentarily suspending their own training to witness the feat. For the poster, still struggling with a single-plate overhead press, the implied timeline to competitive parity stretches, quite literally, into the distant future.

clips.text_en_b1: A /a/ poster calls Yani Neko the greatest work of counterculture art to come out of anime in years. clips.text_en_b2: A /a/ poster makes the case that Yani Neko stands as the most genuinely countercultural piece of anime art to emerge in years. Viewers get worked up over its gross-out humor, sexual comedy, or what they call 'promotion' of drug use, but that reaction only proves they cannot read past the surface. The drugs, bodily fluids, poverty, and raw sexuality depicted are unflinching reflections of reality.
clips.text_en_c1: A provocative thread on /a/ advances the proposition that Yani Neko constitutes the most significant work of countercultural art anime has produced in recent memory. Detractors recoil at its grotesquerie, its unflinching treatment of substance abuse, and what they charitably term its 'promotional' stance toward intoxication, though such reactions merely betray an inability to engage with subtext. The drugs, the bodily fluids, the grinding poverty, the frank sexuality: these are not provocations for their own sake but unflattering mirrors held to social reality. For viewers whose preferences gravitate toward Gundam 00 or Attack on Titan, the work merits reconsideration as something altogether more uncomfortable, and consequently more essential.
clips.text_en_c2: A /a/ poster advances the proposition that Yani Neko constitutes the most consequential work of countercultural art to emerge from the anime medium in the past decade, a claim that predictably provokes both fervent defenders and vociferous detractors. The latter tend to recoil from its transgressive palette of gross-out humour, overt sexuality, and unflinching engagement with substance abuse, dismissing the work as provocation for its own sake. Yet the poster contends, with some justification, that such readings mistake the surface for the substance; the drugs, bodily fluids, grinding poverty, and carnal frankness depicted within are not stylistic affectations but rather faithful renderings of realities that mainstream anime prefers to aestheticise into oblivion. For viewers, the poster included, whose tastes incline toward Gundam 00 and Attack on Titan, the work offers a bracing corrective.
